name: Georgian Service Core
description: The kitchen and its dependencies, kept out of sight and often out of the main block entirely. In the Chesapeake the kitchen is a separate building; in New England it is the rear lean-to. Either way the logic is the same: heat, smell, noise and servants are separated from the formal rooms, and connected by a route no guest uses.

rooms.note: The buffer between service and dining, and the reason the dining room stays clean.

internal_rules.statement: A route from kitchen to dining room that crosses no formal room. This is the rule the whole grouping exists to satisfy.
The back stair is separate from the main stair and lands in the back hall, not on the formal landing.
The larder faces north and has no direct sun. A south-facing larder is a warm cupboard.
Ridge and eave of a service wing sit below the main block, and the drop is legible from the street. A service wing at full height is a second house.
Where the kitchen is detached, the covered way is roofed and not more than about 40 ft — beyond that the food arrives cold and the connection stops being used.

attaches_to.position: one dependency, joined by a hyphen
the rear lean-to — the whole reason the type exists
the first link after the big house

expansion_logic: Add links. The connected farmstead is this grouping taken to its logical end, and each new need becomes a new lower, narrower section.
servicing_strategy: Its own stack, its own water, its own stair. The whole point is that it can run without touching the formal house.

style_variation.note: Kitchen detached in the yard, joined by a covered way. Fire risk and heat, not squeamishness.
Rear lean-to with the kitchen at the centre and the buttery and dairy at the cold ends.
Detached kitchen house in the rear yard, with quarters above.

sources: Waterman, The Dwellings of Colonial America
Hubka, Big House, Little House, Back House, Barn
